Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Microsoft nearly doubled its capital spending in the year to June 2026. Capital spending is money put into long-lived assets, such as data centers. Even so, Microsoft had cash left over.

Friday, Nov 20, was a hard day for AI stocks. Nvidia fell 14.0%, a chip-stock fund (SMH) 10.6% and the Nasdaq 100 fund (QQQ) 5.7%. Microsoft fell 2.8%, less than the S&P 500 fund (SPY), which lost 3.6%.

Source: Microsoft's cash-flow statements, fiscal years ending June 30. "Left over" is cash brought in minus capital spending, buybacks and dividends. A negative "borrowed" means it repaid more debt than it took on.

Microsoft's capital spending reached $116 billion in its last fiscal year, up from $65 billion. It still paid shareholders nearly $49 billion. It also paid down $3 billion of debt. Every other big AI buyer borrowed in the year to September. Microsoft repaid. Then, on Nov. 4, it sold $25 billion of new bonds.

Its interest bill last fiscal year was $3.1 billion. That was less than the $3.3 billion it earned on its cash. The latest quarter, to September, shows the pace rising. Microsoft spent $39.4 billion against $58.0 billion brought in. We follow the other big builders' cash in Big Tech Earned $607 Billion. Where Did It Go?

Microsoft nearly doubled its capital spending and still paid its shareholders nearly $49 billion. If you want your savings to pay you an income, that kind of cash is what to look for. Can Microsoft Spend More Next Year?

Yes, about $39 billion more from its own cash.

Analysts expect sales of $396 billion in the year to June 2027, or fiscal 2027. Microsoft turns about 57 cents of every $1 of sales into cash. On those sales, that is about $224 billion.

Key Takeaways

Insight Holdings Group's newest 13F shows its three biggest new or added positions last quarter were Microsoft, Bloom Energy and a third stock.

All three have fallen since Sept. 30, Bloom Energy by 49%.

Analysts' average targets are well above all three, including 31% upside for Microsoft.

The third stock looks like the best buy of the three at about 3x forward earnings, with estimates still rising.

A fund's 13F shows what it held on the last day of the quarter, and a lot can change after that. All three of Insight Holdings Group's biggest new or added positions, Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), Bloom Energy (BE:NYSE) and a third stock, trade lower today, and two of them are down more than 40%.

Insight filed its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30 on Nov. 16. It lists $1.27 billion of US stocks across 33 positions, so each stock below is cheaper today than it was in that snapshot.

Microsoft is cheaper than its usual multiple

Insight's biggest new position was Microsoft: 160,470 shares worth $82 million at Sept. 30. That's 6.5% of its 13F and its sixth-largest holding. The stock is down 6% since then and sits 13% below its 52-week high.

That leaves Microsoft at about 23x forward earnings. Its 12-year quarter-end average is 26x, and its five-year average is 30x. Analysts have also raised their numbers since October: consensus normalized EPS is now $20.01 for fiscal 2027 (the year to June 2027) and $24.20 for fiscal 2028.

TIKR tracks 58 analysts on Microsoft. Their average target is $636, 31% above the last close, and it has stayed in a narrow band over the past year:

Microsoft (MSFT): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

The worry is cash. Capex reached $115.9 billion in fiscal 2026, and analysts expect free cash flow to fall by about half in fiscal 2027, from $67.0 billion.

Bloom Energy's demand is fine, its stock isn't

Insight added 53% to its Bloom Energy stake in the quarter, ending with 133,925 shares worth $37 million, or 2.9% of its 13F. The stock has dropped 49% since Sept. 30 and is 59% below its 52-week high.

Demand isn't what's hurting the stock. On Oct. 22, Bloom raised its 2026 revenue guidance for the third time, to $4.4 billion to $4.6 billion, after third-quarter revenue jumped 138% to $1.24 billion. Politics did more of the damage: AI power stocks sold off on midterm fears after Democrats won Congress and Texas's incoming governor promised a moratorium on new data-center approvals.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Over the past five years, Dell stock has returned 447%. Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) has returned 220%. So $10,000 put in Dell five years ago is now worth about $54,700. The same amount in HPE is worth about $32,000. Dell and HP were once two similar hardware companies. What did Dell do differently? Was it one big decision, or many small ones?

Both stocks fell hard on Friday, Nov 20, as AI stocks sold off. Dell lost 11.0% and HPE 10.1%, while the S&P 500 fund (SPY) fell 3.6%. The returns below include that drop.

First, the gap. Dell beat HPE over one, three and five years. But HPE also beat the S&P 500 by a wide margin. The slow one is HP Inc, the PC half of the old HP. Over five years, $10,000 grew to about $10,600 in HP Inc. In the S&P 500 it grew to about $15,800.

Source: Trefis, prices through the Nov 20, 2026 close. Total return includes dividends. The S&P 500 is measured by the SPY fund.

Dell stock is up 447% in five years, and HPE 220%. After gains that big, a sharp drop can be hard to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018. It also pays about 3 times the S&P 500's dividend yield. See how it held up.

The Big Decision: Going Private, Then Buying EMC

In 2013 Michael Dell and Silver Lake took Dell private. That means they bought out the public shareholders, so the stock stopped trading. It took Dell out of reach of quarterly pressure over a shrinking PC business. Revenue had fallen from $62.1 billion in fiscal 2012 to $56.9 billion.

In 2016 Michael Dell closed the purchase of EMC, one of the largest tech deals ever. It made Dell a major storage company alongside its servers. Revenue went from $50.9 billion in fiscal 2016 to $78.7 billion two years later. Dell returned to the stock market in 2018. In 2021 it spun off VMware into a separate company. It used a $9.3 billion VMware dividend to pay down debt.

What Did HP Do Instead?

HP went the other way. In fiscal 2006 HP sold $91.7 billion, 1.6 times Dell's $55.8 billion. In 2015 its board split it into HP Inc and HPE. In 2017 HPE shed its services and software arms. Its revenue fell from $50.1 billion to $28.9 billion in a year. In 2025 HPE bought Juniper Networks.

Last fiscal year, Dell's sales of $113.5 billion topped both HP companies combined, at $89.6 billion. One company was rebuilt by its founder. The other was split up by its board.

title: Tech Outages Drive Costco Surge: How Much Emergency Prep Should You Buy?

Tech Outages Drive Costco Surge: How Much Emergency Prep Should You Buy?

Credit: Justin Sullivan / Staff · Getty Images

Bulk essentials and generators were wiped out as shoppers rushed to stock up on emergency supplies. The buying spree follows several widespread outages, including a Microsoft Outlook outage and a nationwide halt for all U.S. airline flights.

The sudden demand surge could also give Costco an unexpected sales boost heading into the holidays, but how much emergency preparation is necessary? Here's what you really need.

Read Next: Get a Free Gold IRA Guide From Forbes' Most Trusted Gold Company

Find Out: FREE 2026 Investor Guide + Up to $25,000 in Silver with Qualifying Purchases

What's Driving the Surge in Panic Buying

According to Mizuho Securities analyst David Bellinger, 21 of the 26 high-priced generators available on Costco's website were sold out as of Sunday night, including whole-home backup systems costing nearly $7,000, Fox Business reported.

Bellinger attributed the increase in emergency preparedness purchases to recent disruptions involving Microsoft Outlook and U.S. airline flights, along with "apocalyptic concerns" on social media.

On Nov. 12, a software issue halted Microsoft Outlook services during peak U.S. business hours, affecting email calendars and meeting invitations. The next day, a separate tech issue involving Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) router installations caused a ground stop to all U.S. flights.

According to the FAA, the disruption resulted in 12,462 canceled flights. The agency has paused additional router installations while investigating the cause.

In an email to Bloomberg, Costco CFO Gary Millerchip also acknowledged the increase in purchases of certain products toward the end of October. Shoppers are buying more rice, canned goods, water, paper products, generators and batteries.

However, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there's "zero evidence" that these recent outages in the U.S. are connected, per CBS News. The affected companies also denied that cyberattacks were responsible.

What It Could Mean for Costco and Other Retailers

The recent increase in emergency preparedness purchases could also boost Costco's November sales.

According to Bellinger, the surge in demand could help Costco achieve double-digit U.S. sales growth in November for the first time since mid-2022.

The retailer was already seeing strong sales heading into November. In its latest monthly sales report, Costco reported $24.50 billion in net sales for October, a 12.6% increase from the same period last year.

Mizuho Securities also raised its price target for Costco shares from $1,100 to $1,150, citing the strength of the recent buying spree as one factor, Bloomberg reported.

Key Takeaways

Castle Hook Partners, a $12 billion fund, opened a new stake in Microsoft and added heavily to Danaher and Thermo Fisher Scientific in the third quarter, per its 13F filed Nov. 16.

The three positions made up nearly 18% of the fund's 13F stocks at Sept. 30.

Analysts' average targets sit 31% above Microsoft's last close, 18% above Danaher's and 13% above Thermo Fisher's.

Microsoft is the one the numbers back best: it trades below its long-run multiple while analysts keep raising their estimates.

Castle Hook Partners, a $12 billion fund, filed its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30 on Nov. 16. Its three biggest moves were a brand-new stake in Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) and much bigger positions in Danaher (DHR:NYSE) and Thermo Fisher Scientific (TMO:NYSE).

Together, those three made up nearly 18% of its 13F stocks at the quarter's end. That's a lot of conviction packed into one software giant and two life-science tools companies.

Microsoft went straight to No. 2

The filing shows 1.72 million Microsoft shares worth $885 million, or 7.1% of its 13F stocks. That makes it the fund's second-largest position. It also raised its Danaher stake 59% to 3.37 million shares, worth $748 million and 6.0% of its 13F stocks, its No. 3. And it added 408% to its Thermo Fisher position, ending the quarter with 843,780 shares worth $570 million, 4.6% of its 13F stocks and its No. 4. (A 13F only shows what a fund held on the quarter's last day, so it says nothing about when Castle Hook bought or what it paid.)

TIKR tracks 58 analysts on Microsoft. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Microsoft, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Microsoft's Analyst Ratings

Microsoft is cheaper than the fund's own snapshot

Microsoft is down 6% since Sept. 30, so anyone following Castle Hook today pays less than the quarter-end price the filing reflects. And the business is giving analysts reasons to raise their numbers. In the September quarter, Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue grew 17% while commercial seats grew 5%, as customers moved up to pricier plans including Copilot. Consensus normalized EPS for fiscal 2027 (the year ending June 2027) is now $20.01, up from $19.76 in late October.

The Street's average target has climbed from a July low of $556 to $636, 31% above the last close:

Microsoft (MSFT): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

On fiscal 2028's $24.20 consensus EPS, that $636 works out to about 26x by my math, right at Microsoft's 12-year average multiple. Today it trades at about 23x forward earnings, below that average and well under the 30x it averaged over the past five years. So Microsoft only needs its estimates to hold to get there. Castle Hook isn't alone, either: Coatue more than doubled its own Microsoft stake in the same quarter.

Buy Microsoft and Amazon at More Than 70x 2028 Free Cash Flow? Here's What Their Capex Must Return ©jiefeng jiang from Getty Images and Quality Stock Arts via Canva
Key Takeaways

At the Nov. 20 close, Microsoft traded at about 77x the free cash flow analysts expect for fiscal 2028, and Amazon traded at about 75x.

Amazon plans to spend about $220 billion on capex this year and more next year, and analysts expect its free cash flow to stay negative until 2028.

At 30x free cash flow, both would need far more cash than they've ever made, and the capex peak that gets them there could slow Arista Networks.

Microsoft's contracted backlog makes its bet easier to trust than Amazon's.

Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) CEO Andy Jassy has no plans to slow down. Asked on CNBC's Halftime Report on Nov. 17 about Wall Street's capex forecasts, he said "we expect to spend around $220 billion this year in CapEx and that we expect to spend meaningfully more next year."

A lot of that money becomes revenue for suppliers like Arista Networks (ANET:NYSE).

One investor in r/ValueInvesting argued that Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) and Amazon trade at more than 80 times estimated fiscal 2028 free cash flow.

TIKR's estimates backed that up at the Nov. 18 close. Then two days of tech selling took about 5% off Microsoft and 8% off Amazon. Both now trade below 80x, but still above 70x.

Still More Than 70x

At the Nov. 20 close, Microsoft was worth about $3.60 trillion, or about 77x the $46.8 billion of free cash flow analysts expect in its fiscal 2028. They see free cash flow falling by more than half in fiscal 2027 and then recovering only partway:

Microsoft (MSFT): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2028 (years to June) (TIKR)

Capex explains the drop. Microsoft's cash capital spending rose to $115.9 billion in fiscal 2026 from $64.6 billion, and analysts expect $193.7 billion in fiscal 2027.

Amazon was worth about $2.67 trillion, or about 75x the $35.7 billion of free cash flow analysts expect in 2028. To get there, it first goes through two years of negative free cash flow:

Amazon (AMZN): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2028 (TIKR)

Its capex rose to $132 billion in 2025 from $52.7 billion in 2023:

Amazon (AMZN): capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Jassy's $220 billion for this year is roughly 1.7x that.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Microsoft, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Microsoft's Analyst Ratings

What the capex has to return

Say you'd pay 30x free cash flow, still a premium price. At Nov. 20 values, Microsoft would need about $120 billion a year, about 1.6x the $74.1 billion it made in fiscal 2024, its best year on the chart. Amazon would need about $89 billion a year, roughly 2.3x its 2024 figure of $38.2 billion. Neither has ever come close.

Wall Street's artificial intelligence trade is looking considerably less comfortable than it did a few months ago. Technology stocks that once commanded premium valuations for their AI ambitions are losing ground as investors question whether trillions of dollars in infrastructure spending will produce adequate returns.

Photo by Astrid Stawiarz/Getty Images

The selling has spread from semiconductor manufacturers to the companies building and renting AI data centers. Even strong earnings reports have struggled to restore confidence.

For investors who spent the past year watching AI stocks climb, the reversal has been painful. But for Michael Burry, the hedge fund manager famous for predicting the 2008 housing collapse, it's looking remarkably familiar.

Michael Burry Says He Warned Investors

On Nov. 19, Burry took to X to remind investors of his previous warnings about Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS), and semiconductor stocks.

"I tried to warn you all," Burry wrote on X, adding, "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."

The timing was deliberate. Nvidia fell 3.3% that Thursday, while CoreWeave declined 6.1%, and Nebius plunged 9.4%. The damage extends well beyond one trading session.
